What would you see,
and what would you feel,
if you fell into a black hole?
Imagine drifting toward a
supermassive one in a spacecraft,
with a friend watching from far away.
One of you will see something very
different from the other.
Take a quiet look at the palm

Feel the steady, invisible weight
pulling your fingers down toward the floor.
You live inside an ocean of gravity

What if you pushed that familiar
pull to its absolute breaking point,
and stepped directly into the dark
mouth of a black hole?
Most of us imagine a black hole
as a terrifying cosmic vacuum
cleaner roaming the universe.
But the reality painted by modern
physics is far stranger,
far quieter, and infinitely more
eerie than any monster you could imagine.
A black hole does not violently
chase you across the cosmos.
Instead, it simply waits,
bending the fabric of space and
time into a bottomless slope.
If you drifted too close,
the universe would not tear you
apart with loud explosions.
It would rewrite your reality,
sentence by sentence, until your
very future ceased to exist.
